The True Hall of Fame — the same yardstick for every player who ever played.

Ranked on the field, not on ballots.

Welcome to The True Hall Of Fame — a virtual hall for the MLB players whose careers, measured by the statistics they piled up, put them among the best ever to play the game. Membership is decided by a single formula built from box-score facts: a player's Stat Above Average (SAA), the same calculation applied to everyone. There's no five-year waiting period and no requirement to be retired — active players are eligible. Every player here earned the ticket on the field.

The museum in Cooperstown, New York is a wonderful place — artifacts from every era and a gallery of plaques for the players voted in. And that's the operative word: voted. Induction is an honor decided by ballot, with the writers and the era committees weighing each candidate and casting a yes or a no. That's a legitimate way to run a hall of fame, it's the one they chose, and they've never claimed the vote is beyond dispute. But a ballot is a judgment call, and judgment varies — from writer to writer, and from one era's standards to the next. In our view, that has left the results inconsistent enough to be worth a second look on the numbers alone. Some of what that looks like:

Hank Aaron was elected in his first year on the ballot, as he should have been — but not unanimously. He was named on 406 of 415 ballots, 97.8%. Nine writers left the game's all-time home run leader off entirely. Willie Mays drew 94.7%. Ted Williams, 93.4%. You can argue any single omission; it's harder to explain why the inner-circle greats face meaningful opposition at all.

The first player ever elected unanimously wasn't Babe Ruth, Ty Cobb, or Walter Johnson. It was Mariano Rivera, in 2019. Of everyone in the Hall, exactly one has been named on every ballot. One.

And the voting doesn't track production cleanly. Bobby Grich (71.1 career WAR) and Lou Whitaker (75.1) are on the outside looking in, while Harold Baines (38.7) and Tommy McCarthy (14.7) are in.

None of this makes Cooperstown wrong — it's their hall, run their way, by rules they're entitled to set. But in our view the process is broken in a specific way: it's inconsistent, and it shifts with who is voting and when. So we built the other version — one transparent formula, applied identically to every player in history, with no ballots and no committees. That's The True Hall of Fame.

The True Hall of Fame — hitters, part one of two

Top 300 Hitters by Stat Above Average

This isn't trying to reproduce who's actually in Cooperstown — it's this project's own answer to who belongs. No linear-weight run values, no replacement-level constant: every player is scored only against the actual league average and spread of their own season, using five genuinely separate things you can point to directly in a box score — batting average, isolated power, walk rate, stolen-base rate, and defensive value.

143 / 300also in Cooperstown

This is a living ranking, not a set of plaques. It's rebuilt from scratch every year on the latest data, so a player climbs onto the list when his case passes the 300th, and a borderline name drops off when someone else's rises past him. Active players are in — no five-year wait. What you're looking at is the 2025 edition; the twenty names just outside the cut are listed at the bottom.

What's a Stat Above Average? Each player-season is compared only to that season's own league average and spread — a 1927 season is judged against 1927, a 2024 season against 2024, nothing crosses eras. The five stats above are each converted to a z-score (standard deviations above or below that year's league mean, computed from qualifying hitters only) and blended into one number for the season: batting average and isolated power at 30% each, defense at 20%, walk rate and stolen-base rate at 10% each. (Walks and steals are both dialed back — a walks-only bat or a pure basestealer could each otherwise ride one category onto the list ahead of a complete hitter; leaning the score on contact and power pulls the list closer to the actual Hall of Fame.)

The career number blends length and peak. A player's season scores, each scaled to a 600-PA workload, are summed into a career total — but a great career cut short shouldn't be buried under compilers, so the ranking metric is the average of that career total and the sum of the player's best seven seasons (the same career-plus-peak shape JAWS uses). Play a long time and at a high level and both halves are large.

Negro Leagues players qualify on a separate standard, not the 5,000 PA floor — their official league schedules were far shorter than MLB's, and the surviving record undercounts them further still. They qualify instead by accumulating the equivalent of 9 seasons at their own league's typical season size — the standard that gets Josh Gibson, Willie Wells, and Turkey Stearnes onto this list. The NeL flag beside a player's rank marks the ones whose score actually draws on Negro Leagues play — a 200-plus-PA season in a Negro Major League — not a brief cameo like Willie Mays's 13 games in 1948.

Runs scored and RBI were deliberately left out — both depend heavily on who's on base ahead of you and where you hit in the order, not just your own output. The HOF column marks players the writers and veterans committees have already voted into Cooperstown, so you can see at a glance where this list and the official one agree and where they don't.

Where the list and your gut disagree

Two it leaves out

Alan Trammell and Derek Jeter are both Hall of Fame shortstops, and the list treats them nothing alike — Trammell is 301st, one name out; Jeter is 431st, a hundred and thirty out. On Trammell the formula basically agrees with the room: a fine all-around career, genuinely borderline. On Jeter it stands alone.

#301 Alan Trammell SS · 1977–1996 · DET

.285 AVG · 110 OPS+ · 2,365 H · 185 HR · 236 SB · 70.7 bWAR

AVG+0.63
ISO-0.12
BB+0.04
SB+0.18
DEF+0.25

A z-line that clears zero across the board and never reaches +0.7 anywhere: a little above his leagues at contact, roughly average power, patience, speed and a slightly positive glove — the shape this score respects, but here it just runs out of seasons at the wrong moment. He is the case for a floating list: one strong year from an active shortstop and he's in; a Negro Leagues data revision and he's out. Right now, 301st.

#431 Derek Jeter SS · 1995–2014 · NYY

.310 AVG · 115 OPS+ · 3,465 H · 260 HR · 358 SB · 71.3 bWAR

AVG+1.32
ISO-0.54
BB-0.12
SB+0.67
DEF-1.02

3,465 hits, five titles, a first-ballot plaque at 99.7% — and the two categories weighted 30% each both go the wrong way. Elite contact (+1.32), but no power for a modern star (−0.54 ISO) and a range metric that graded him a full standard deviation below the line at short for two decades. Twenty years of it doesn't rescue a per-season rate that thin. The formula measures what it measures; here it and the whole sport disagree, loudly: 431st.

At 143 of the 300, this is the closest the list has come to Cooperstown — the expansion mostly pulled in catchers the range metric can't see (Yogi Berra, Iván Rodríguez, Ted Simmons, Gary Carter) and long all-around careers the old 200-man cut left just outside (Lou Whitaker, Craig Biggio, Ichiro). What it still won't do is bend for a profile it genuinely disagrees with — Jeter, Omar Vizquel (896th), Brooks Robinson (334th). That's the point.

Recalculated every year

On the bubble

The twenty just outside the cut, ranks 301–320. A strong season from an active player, a shift in the Negro Leagues record, or the next weighting pass, and the line moves.

SAA = a weighted blend of five per-season z-scores — batting average [H/AB] and isolated power [SLG−AVG] at 30% each, defensive value [range runs + positional credit] at 20%, walk rate [BB/PA] and stolen-base rate [SB/PA] at 10% each — against that season's league mean and spread among 200+ PA hitters, each season scaled to 600 PA. The ranking number is the average of the career total and the sum of the player's best seven seasons. Pool: 5,000+ career PA (or, for Negro Leagues players, 9+ seasons normalized to their own league's typical season size). Source: Lahman database hitting/fielding (2025 release, including Negro Leagues statistics); Hall of Fame membership current through the 2026 induction class.

How Stat Above Average works

One formula, applied identically whether you struck people out or drove them in.

A hitter's Stat Above Average (SAA) is built one season at a time. Each season, five rate stats are turned into z-scores — standard deviations above or below that season's league average, measured against qualifying hitters only — then blended by weight, scaled to a 600‑plate‑appearance workload, and summed across the whole career. The ranking number is a JAWS-style 50/50 average of that career total and the sum of the player's seven best individual seasons, so a long steady career and a short brilliant one can both build a real case.

Hitters = 30% AVG vs league + 30% ISO vs league + 20% Defense vs position + 10% Walk rate vs league + 10% Steal rate vs league

A pitcher's SAA works the same way, minus the peak adjustment: five z-scored rate stats per season (ERA and WHIP flipped, so beating the league counts as positive), blended by weight, scaled to a 200‑inning workload, and summed across every qualifying season. There is no best-seven bonus — a pitcher's number is the career total only.

Pitchers = 25% ERA vs league + 25% WHIP vs league + 20% K/9 vs league + 20% Win% + 10% Saves vs league

Every comparison is to the player's own league in the exact seasons he played — a 1927 season is judged against 1927, a 2024 season against 2024. A career that spans eras gets a benchmark blended across those years. Nothing is measured against a fixed all-time standard or a replacement‑level constant. The weights are deliberately tilted toward contact, power, and run prevention: a walks-only bat or a pure basestealer could otherwise ride a single category past a complete player.

Glossary

Every abbreviation you'll run into on the lists, the cards, and the Stats pages.

The five hitting inputs

AVG — Batting average
Hits divided by at‑bats. The oldest measure of pure contact.
ISO — Isolated power
Slugging percentage minus batting average: extra bases per at‑bat, with singles stripped out. A hitter with nothing but singles has an ISO of .000; prime Babe Ruth sat around .350.
Defense (vs position)
Runs saved or cost relative to an average fielder at the same position in the same era, built from putouts and assists against the positional rate and scaled by playing time. A shortstop is only ever compared to other shortstops.
Walk rate (BB)
Bases on balls as a share of plate appearances — how often a hitter reaches base without putting the ball in play.
Steal rate (SB)
Net stolen‑base value per plate appearance: steals credited, caught‑stealing charged at a heavier penalty. Weighted lightly on purpose.

The five pitching inputs

ERA — Earned run average
Earned runs allowed per nine innings. Lower is better, so the z‑score is flipped before it's blended.
WHIP — Walks and hits per inning pitched
Baserunners allowed per inning, walks plus hits. Also flipped — fewer is better.
K/9 — Strikeouts per nine innings
The one bat‑missing skill that shows up on every stat sheet, in any era.
Win% — Winning percentage
Wins divided by decisions (wins plus losses). It leans on the team around the pitcher, so it carries a modest weight.
SV — Saves
Games finished protecting a lead, per the official rule. Weighted lightest of the five: it depends heavily on how a manager chooses to use a pitcher.

Other batting stats on the site

OBP — On‑base percentage
Times reached base (hits + walks + hit‑by‑pitch) divided by plate appearances.
SLG — Slugging percentage
Total bases divided by at‑bats — a double counts 2, a home run 4.
OPS — On‑base plus slugging
OBP + SLG. A quick catch‑all for offensive value; .900 and up is star level.
OPS+ — Adjusted OPS
OPS restated so 100 is league average and each point above is one percent better, adjusted for ballpark. 150 means 50% better than league.
PA — Plate appearances
Every trip to the plate, walks and sacrifices included. SAA scales each hitting season to 600 PA.
R, RBI, HR, H, 2B, 3B, SB, BB, SO
Runs, runs batted in, home runs, hits, doubles, triples, stolen bases, walks, strikeouts — raw season and career totals, no adjustment.

Other pitching stats on the site

IP — Innings pitched
Shown in the traditional thirds notation: 200.1 is 200 innings and one out, 200.2 is two outs. SAA scales each pitching season to 200 IP.
ERA+ — Adjusted ERA
ERA restated to a 100‑is‑average, park‑adjusted scale where higher is better — the inverse direction of raw ERA.
W, L, G, GS, CG, SHO
Wins, losses, games, games started, complete games, shutouts.
H, ER, HR, BB, SO (allowed)
Hits, earned runs, home runs, walks, and strikeouts a pitcher gave up.

Methodology terms

z‑score
How far a number sits from the average, measured in standard deviations. A z of +1 is one standard deviation better than that season's qualifying players; +2 is rare air. SAA blends z‑scores, not raw stats, so separating yourself in a tightly bunched category counts for more than in one where the league is spread all over.
“vs league” / league‑relative
Every input is scored against the average of the same season, never a fixed all‑time bar. This is the core difference from career‑counting totals and from WAR's replacement level.
Qualifying season
A season that counts toward SAA: 200+ plate appearances for a hitter, 40+ innings for a pitcher. Below the line, a season doesn't move the number.
Peak / best‑seven
For hitters, the final SAA is a 50/50 average of the career total and the sum of the seven best individual seasons — the same idea as Baseball‑Reference's JAWS. It stops a compiler with no great years from outranking a shorter‑career great. Pitchers get no peak component.
WAR / bWAR
Wins Above Replacement, the mainstream all‑in‑one value stat. “bWAR” is Baseball‑Reference's version, the one quoted on this site. See Why not WAR? below.
Replacement level
The baseline WAR measures against: what a team could get essentially for free from the minor leagues or the waiver wire. SAA has no equivalent — it compares to the real league, not a hypothetical floor.
NeL
A flag on the lists marking a player whose SAA draws on Negro Leagues seasons — now part of the official record and scored exactly the same way.
Cooperstown / HOF
The Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York, and its membership, which is decided by vote. The HOF column on each list shows who is already in.

Why not WAR?

Wins Above Replacement measures every player against one universal "replacement level" — a theoretical bench player, calibrated once from decades of injury-substitution data and then applied identically to a dead-ball-era outfielder and a modern closer. It's the industry standard for good reason, but that one number was never derived for either of them specifically.

Stat Above Average measures every player against their own competition instead — the actual league average, in the actual years and at the actual position they played, blended across whichever eras their career spans.

No replacement level. No runs-to-wins conversion borrowed from someone else's research. Just each player's rate stats, held up against the players who were actually on the field around them.
